newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel sees "common way" with Buba on reserves.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel sees "common way" with Buba on reserves.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday he and the Bundesbank had agreed on a common approach to revalue assets to help Bonn's drive to join the European single currency but gave parliament few details.

Addressing a parliament session due to vote on an opposition resolution to sack him, Waigel said he and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer would do their best to have windfall revaluation profits transfered to Bonn's budget from 1998.
Waigel, who wanted profits from revalued gold reserves to give him much-needed funds in 1997 as part of Germany's bid to qualify for Europe's monetary union (EMU), said no bullion would be sold.

But he did not make it clear whether gold or currency reserves or both were to be revalued. Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer has said the gold reserves were not under discussion during his talks with Waigel in Bonn on Tuesday.

"We have found a common way," said Waigel, who on Tuesday admitted he had a gap of at least 19 billion marks ($11 billion) in his 1997 budget and would have to privatise and cut spending more this year to fill it.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right government caved in to enormous Bundesbank pressure on Tuesday and dropped a plan to change the central bank's law and force it to pay out new profits from revalued gold and currency reserves.

Waigel, in fighting mood as he opened the stormy session of parliament, also said Germany would still be able to meet the three percent deficit-to-GDP Maastricht target despite the delay in getting extra funds from the Bundesbank.

He also repeated Bonn's long-standing insistence on a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria, a position whose credibility the unprecedented Bonn-Bundesbank feud of the past week has seriously weakened.

Rudolf Scharping, parliamentary leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), accused Waigel of trying to deceive German voters by giving the impression he had an agreement with the Bundesbank while the Frankfurt-based bank's council still had to approve its details.
"This policy has reached its end -- you must leave office!" he told Waigel. "This government has become a heavy burden for Germany." ($ = 1.731 German Marks)
